Living Well / Essay

When does documenting your life get in the way of experiencing it?

Essay · 3 min read · Published October 8, 2026

On this page
  1. Decide what the recording is for
  2. Keep participation and production distinct
  3. Choose a boundary before the moment disappears
  4. Technology can support the record without owning the memory
  5. A record should remain usable
  6. One question to take with you

By Nolan Kido · About this writing

Making a record can be an act of attention. It can also turn a moment into material before you have had a chance to live it. The useful question is where the boundary belongs.

Decide what the recording is for

A private keepsake, a creative project, and a public update ask different things of a moment. Before recording, identify the purpose. You may need only a brief visual reference, a short passage of sound, or no recording at all.

This is not an argument against photography or video. Making something can deepen your engagement with a subject. But the fact that an experience can be recorded does not establish that it should become content, particularly when other people are part of it.

Keep participation and production distinct

Consider a hypothetical visit with a friend. Taking one agreed photograph is different from repeatedly interrupting the conversation to get the scene right. Both activities may be enjoyable when everyone understands the purpose, but they are not the same kind of visit.

Be clear about which activity is happening. A person who agreed to spend time with you did not necessarily agree to appear in a public story. Ask rather than interpreting their willingness to be photographed as permission for every later use.

Choose a boundary before the moment disappears

You might decide to record an opening scene and then put the camera away, or to reserve a part of an outing for making images. A boundary can protect both activities: the creative work gets attention, and the rest of the experience does not have to keep justifying its value as footage.

Leave room to change your mind. The planned image may become intrusive or simply no longer seem worth making. Missing a shot is not the same as missing the experience. A moment that remains private is not necessarily a lost opportunity.

Technology can support the record without owning the memory

Tools may help organize files, locate an approved excerpt, or make a transcript easier to review. Those tasks should preserve the distinction between what happened and what has been edited or generated. Do not fill a gap in a real memory with synthetic detail and present it as documentation.

When sharing, keep context and consent in view. An isolated excerpt can imply something the fuller exchange did not. Ask whether the edit remains fair to the people involved, not only whether it makes the story more compelling.

A record should remain usable

A large collection is not automatically an accessible one. A few well-described files or a short sequence you can find again may serve the purpose better than indiscriminate accumulation. Choose an organization method that you can realistically maintain.

The same principle applies to attention. You do not need to preserve every moment to honor it. Some experiences may be better carried as a conversation, a practice, or a changed understanding rather than another file.

One optional practice

Before one ordinary outing or creative session, decide what you would like to record and what you would like to leave unrecorded. Treat the boundary as adjustable, and ask permission where other people are involved.

Keep any notes privately. Skip or adapt this exercise if it does not fit your circumstances.

One question to take with you

What would you still value about this experience if there were no image or story to share afterwards?
